detail:
Amazon (AMZN) Is A Proven Capital Allocator. But Can it Pass Its $220 Billion Test?
Sanmit Amin

AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) has been flat during the last six months, as of October 15. This compares to a 21.5% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 15.74% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Amazon has a history of building businesses that eventually become valuable in their own right. AWS started with the infrastructure Amazon needed to run its website, while advertising grew out of the traffic coming to its online store. Now, the company is looking for similar opportunities with its custom chips and logistics network. The strategy has worked before, but Amazon is spending on a much larger scale this time. The big question is whether these investments will deliver returns that justify the cost.

Amazon ranks 1st in our list of 10 Best Stocks to Buy for the Next 20 Years. Click HERE to find out other stocks on the list.

Amazon (AMZN) Is A Proven Capital Allocator. But Can it Pass Its a $220 Billion Test
Amazon Keeps Finding New Ways to Grow

Amazon Supply Chain Services, launched in May, allows outside companies to use its freight, distribution, fulfillment, and parcel delivery network. Procter & Gamble, 3M, Lands' End and American Eagle were among its first customers. The company is taking a similar approach with its Trainium and Graviton chips, which were developed for AWS but could eventually find customers beyond Amazon's own cloud.

The attraction is easy to understand. Amazon has already spent years building these capabilities, so selling them to outside customers creates another way to earn money from that investment. But there is a difference between cloud computing and logistics. Every additional shipment brings costs for labor, transportation, and handling. The business will only make sense if Amazon can attract enough customers to generate profits without disrupting deliveries to its own shoppers.

AMZN ranked 1st in our list of the 10 Most Active Blue Chip Stocks to Buy Right Now. To see which other stocks made the list, click HERE.

AI Could Drive More Than Chip Demand

AWS has more to gain from AI than simply selling computing power to companies developing models. AI applications also need storage, databases, security, and the computing resources required to run them in everyday business operations. Bedrock allows customers to choose from different AI models, while multi-year commitments from Anthropic and OpenAI give Amazon another route to benefit from demand for Trainium. It does not necessarily need to develop the industry's leading model to make money from AI.

Cloud migration offers another opportunity. CEO Andy Jassy has pointed out that much of the world's IT spending is still tied to on-premises infrastructure. As companies move more of their systems to the cloud, AWS could benefit even if their AI adoption takes longer than expected. Not all that spending will go to Amazon, of course, but it gives the company another source of potential growth.

title: 2 Retail Stocks to Buy Before the Holiday Shopping Season

2 Retail Stocks to Buy Before the Holiday Shopping Season
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool

AMZN
NVDA
COST

Thanksgiving is Nov. 26 this year, with Black Friday the day after.

For the largest retailers, the weeks that follow can do more for the year's results than any other stretch. Last year, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) reported fourth-quarter sales around 18% higher than its third-quarter sales.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Two retail stocks look worth owning before the rush to me: Amazon and Costco Wholesale (NASDAQ:COST). Both are going into the season with sales growth that has held up well this year.

But their stocks have gone different ways lately. Amazon shares are still well below the record they hit in early August. Costco shares, meanwhile, have risen around 8% so far in October to near $1,000 as I write.

Image source: Amazon.

1. Amazon's biggest quarter is coming

Amazon's fourth quarter is reliably its biggest. In the holiday period of 2025, net sales hit $213.4 billion, 14% higher than a year before and far above the third quarter's $180.2 billion.

The profits show up in the retail business, too. Operating income for Amazon's North America segment, which has most of its store sales, rose around 24% year over year to $11.5 billion in last year's fourth quarter. That was far above the third quarter's $7.3 billion (a number that leaves out a $2.5 billion legal settlement with the Federal Trade Commission).

And this year, Amazon's sales have risen even faster. Revenue growth picked up from 14% in last year's fourth quarter to 17% in this year's first quarter, then 20% in the second, but Prime Day's move to June lifted that final number.

Of course, the same shift holds back the third quarter. Management's outlook calls for growth of 9% to 12%, or about 13% to 16% with Prime Day left out in both years. The third-quarter report, probably due later this month, should also have management's first forecast for the holiday quarter.

Even after a rise of about 2% in October, the stock trades near $254, about 11% below the $284.02 record close it set Aug. 3.

Based on analysts' 2027 earnings estimates, shares cost about 24 times earnings. This looks like a fair price to me for a company going into its biggest quarter with double-digit sales growth.

2. Costco is entering the holidays growing faster

The warehouse club's fiscal first quarter spans 12 weeks ending right before Thanksgiving, so Black Friday and December fall in Costco's fiscal second quarter. This makes its monthly sales reports the first public look at how the season goes.

Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) reports Q3 2026 earnings on Oct. 29. The e-commerce and cloud giant has benefited from a stable e-commerce business and AI-driven growth.

However, the company pledged $220 billion in capital expenditures (capex) for this year. That staggering sum has strained its finances. Investors are wondering where the capex budget goes from here.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Still, it could pay to buy the leading e-commerce stock before the report.

Image source: Amazon.

The previous three Q3 reports explain why. Each time the company released these Q3 reports in late October, the stock has risen significantly the next day.

Admittedly, this is not a guarantee, as an earnings miss in Q4 of last year led to a decline after the announcement. Also, as previously mentioned, shareholders have become increasingly concerned about Amazon's high capex.

More than a seasonal pattern

Nonetheless, investors should remember that a recession-resistant e-commerce business bolsters Amazon. While the retail part is low margin, it has driven growth by offering digital advertising, subscriptions, and third-party seller services.

Also, despite the e-commerce performance, the focus remains on the AI-driven cloud arm, Amazon Web Services (AWS). Despite making up just 21% of its Q2 revenue, it accounted for the majority of its operating income. Moreover, AWS revenue grew by 37% annually in the latest quarter, up from 17.5% yearly in the year-ago quarter.

Such a result makes Amazon hard to ignore right now.

Finally, there's valuation. A $53.4 billion pre-tax gain on Amazon's Anthropic investment inflated Q2 net income, pushing the trailing P/E down to 20. The forward P/E of 31 is the more meaningful figure, and it's low compared with past years when Amazon routinely traded above 50 times earnings.

The forward P/E ratio of 31 is still low compared to past years when Amazon routinely traded above 50 times earnings. Such conditions increase the likelihood of a favorable reaction to the earnings report.

In an uncertain environment for AI stocks, anything can happen. Nonetheless, if history is any indication, Amazon stock is probably a buy ahead of the company's Oct. 29 after-the-bell report.

Pinterest Stock Is Down 18% This Year. Buy, Sell or Hold? ©Kaspars Grinvalds and IncrediVFX from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Pinterest stock is down 17.5% this year at $21.91, but it has rallied 19.9% from its September 9 close of $18.28.

Holds now lead the Street's ratings: 19 Holds against 17 Buys and 2 Outperforms. The $29.05 mean target sits 32.6% above the close and hasn't moved since September 30.

Q2 revenue rose 18% to $1.18 billion, but the Q3 guide of $1.19 billion to $1.21 billion implies 13% to 15% growth.

A new CFO, Amazon's James Dibbo, starts October 26.

PINS Stock Price: Year-to-Date (TIKR)

Pinterest (PINS:NYSE) stock has lost 17.5% since early January, closing at $21.91 on October 16. Its worst day of the year came on February 13, when a fourth-quarter miss and a soft first-quarter outlook sent shares down 16.8%.

The past five weeks run the other way. Pinterest stock hit a late-summer low close of $18.28 on September 9 and has climbed 19.9% since, by my math, even after a 3.52% drop on October 16. Wall Street hasn't moved with it: the mean analyst target was $29.05 on September 30, and it's $29.05 now.

Pinterest Stock Hit Bottom on February 13

The slide started before earnings and included a January 27 plan to cut just under 15% of the workforce. Pinterest stock closed at $18.54 on February 12, already down 28.4% from its $25.89 year-end close.

Then came the Q4 report. Revenue of $1.319 billion missed the $1.329 billion LSEG consensus. The Q1 guide of $951 million to $971 million landed below the $981 million analysts expected. Stifel tied weak spending by large U.S. and Canadian retailers to tariff pressure. Pinterest stock closed at $15.42 on February 13, down 40.4% for the year in six weeks.

Elliott's $1 Billion Bet and a Softer Q3 Guide

On March 3, Pinterest announced a $1 billion investment from Elliott in convertible notes with an initial conversion price of about $22.72 a share, funding a buyback inside a new $3.5 billion program. Pinterest stock rose 9.3% that day, climbed back above $22 by early May and reached the mid-$25s by early August.

Q2 then sent mixed signals. Revenue rose 18% to $1.18 billion, with U.S. and Canada growth accelerating five points to 18%. But the Q3 guide of $1.19 billion to $1.21 billion implied 13% to 15% growth, and the stock slipped to the low $23s.

Monetization is still the gap. "We 5x the number of clicks to advertisers over that last 3-year period, but we certainly didn't 5x the revenue," CEO Bill Ready said on the Q2 2026 earnings call.

PINS Gave Back the Summer, Then Took Some of It Back

After the close on August 28, Pinterest disclosed that CFO Julia Donnelly would step down. Pinterest stock fell 6.4% to $21.71 on August 31 and kept sliding to that $18.28 close on September 9.

Railroads transformed America and fiber optic cable built the internet, yet many investors who funded both lost money. In a note reported on October 16, 2026, Bank of America investment strategist Sebastian Raedler argued AI is tracking the same path, writing that "most major capital cycles of the past have ended in disappointment, even though the underlying technology often lived up to expectations."

24/7 Wall St.

Raedler argues that AI's technology can succeed while investors in AI stocks still earn poor returns. Sebastian Raedler said 12-month forward consensus hyperscaler capex expectations rose from $330 billion in early 2025 to $1 trillion. Those figures forecast spending by the largest cloud operators over the next year.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 2.5%, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index posted its eighth straight loss, its longest run since 2008. After Bank of America's note, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) slid 1.43% to $214.13, a market value of $5.17 trillion. On Raedler's warning, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) fell 1.93% to $529.05, and its market value slipped below $4 trillion to $3.93 trillion.

How Capital Cycles Punish Investors

In a capital cycle, strong profits pull in a wave of investment until capacity exceeds demand. Prices then fall as competitors fight for customers, and returns on capital sink.
